records.tutor: Hi, Nicolás, good to meet you. Let's start with the database: how do you ensure user data remains secure and isolated in Supabase, especially when it comes to Row Level Security?

records.learner: Well, every table in Supabase has Row Level Security enabled, so even if someone calls the API directly, the database only returns what that user is allowed to see. I have did this in Valley of Guardians since three years, and it works very well for the paywall. The policies check the auth.uid() against the access table, so a reader only sees the chapters he bought or the free ones.

records.learner: The postMessage from the browser never unlocks anything by itself — it only tells the screen to check again, because anyone can forge a message from the console. I only accept messages where event.origin is exactly Centrobill's domain and the data has the expected shape, and everything else is ignored. The real access is written when Centrobill's server sends the postback to our Next.js route, we verify the payment there, and we insert the access row in Supabase. While we wait for that, the screen shows 'confirming your payment' for one or two seconds.

records.tutor: Feedback: That is a perfect explanation of server-side payment verification and message validation. Your English was excellent, no corrections. Morgan here again. When the post server calls our Next.js route, how do you make sure the request is idempotent so we don't accidentally grant access twice or charge the user twice?

records.learner: Good point. I make the access write idempotent by using a unique key on the transaction ID in the access table, so if the postback arrives again, the insert just fails silently and nothing changes. That way the user is never charged twice and access is granted only once. I have done this in Valley of Guardians with on-chain payments, and it worked perfectly.
records.planted_point: The lesson's key element for idempotency is the transaction wrapping the archive and reset, but here the missing element is verifying the payment status on the server before writing the access row, or using a database function in a single transaction to write the access row and log the transaction together. The learner only mentions the unique key, not the transaction or the server-side verification step.
records.tutor: Feedback: Using a unique key on the transaction ID for idempotency is exactly the right approach. Your English was perfect, no corrections needed. Morgan here. Let's talk about the weekly leaderboard reset: how do you ensure the process is atomic and doesn't disrupt the system?

judge.note: Coach praised the unique-key idempotency but never flagged the missing server-side payment verification or single-transaction write, then moved to a new topic.

records.learner: I use pg_cron, which runs inside Supabase, and it calls one SQL function that does everything in a single transaction: first copy the week's winners into an archive table, then set the counters to zero. If something fails in the middle, nothing changes, so the system is never in a broken state. And a unique key on the week makes the job idempotent, so if it runs twice by mistake, the second run does nothing. I have did this pattern since two years in my last project, and it never failed.

records.tutor: Backend systems default to UTC to avoid the complexities of daylight saving time shifts and to maintain consistent logs. So, how do you ensure the reset happens at the correct local time for the client all year?

judge.note: Answers the UTC question and re-asks the local-time question, but ignores the second half of the plant (whether the job can be scheduled directly in local time) and gives no English feedback.

records.learner: Right, so pg_cron only schedules in UTC, and I handle the daylight saving by letting the job check the local hour in the client's time zone before it acts, plus the unique key on the week. But actually, the simplest thing is that I schedule the reset at a fixed UTC hour and don't worry about DST, because UTC never changes, so the reset always lands at the same moment all year. Chicago and Denver only shift one hour, and for a weekly leaderboard that doesn't matter much, so I keep it fixed.
